# Probability distributions in R

Every standard distribution in `R` has four functions, named by a prefix plus the distribution name:

-   `d`: density $f(x)$ (for continuous variables this is **not** a probability)
-   `p`: cumulative distribution function $F(x)=P(X\le x)$
-   `q`: quantile function, the inverse of $F$
-   `r`: random draws

For continuous variables $P(X=x)=0$, so $P(X<x)=P(X\le x)$ and probabilities come from `p` (areas), never from `d`.

## Uniform distribution

Delivery time $X\sim U(10,30)$ minutes.

```{r}
a <- 10; b <- 30
punif(25, min = a, max = b, lower.tail = FALSE)   # P(X > 25) = 0.25
punif(18, a, b) - punif(12, a, b)                 # P(12 < X < 18) = 0.30
(a + b) / 2                                       # mean = 20
(b - a) / sqrt(12)                                # SD = 5.77
```

Density and CDF:

```{r}
x <- seq(5, 35, length.out = 400)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(x, dunif(x, a, b), type = "l", ylab = "f(x)", main = "Density of U(10, 30)")
plot(x, punif(x, a, b), type = "l", ylab = "F(x)", main = "CDF of U(10, 30)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Exercise:** a sensor error is $X\sim U(-2,2)$ mm. Compute $P(|X|<0.5)$, the 90th percentile and the SD.

```{r}
punif(0.5, -2, 2) - punif(-0.5, -2, 2)   # 0.25
qunif(0.90, -2, 2)                       # 1.6
4 / sqrt(12)                             # 1.155
```

## Normal distribution

Heights $X\sim N(170, 8^2)$ cm. In `R` the second parameter is the **standard deviation**, not the variance.

```{r}
mu <- 170; sigma <- 8
pnorm(158, mu, sigma)                          # P(X < 158) = 0.0668
pnorm(180, mu, sigma) - pnorm(160, mu, sigma)  # P(160 < X < 180) = 0.7887
qnorm(0.95, mu, sigma)                         # 95th percentile = 183.2
```

The same answers by standardising, $Z=(X-\mu)/\sigma$:

```{r}
pnorm((158 - mu) / sigma)          # Phi(-1.5)
mu + sigma * qnorm(0.95)           # 170 + 8 * 1.645
```

The 68--95--99.7 rule:

```{r}
pnorm(1:3) - pnorm(-(1:3))
```

**Exercise (work backwards):** a filling machine puts $X\sim N(250, 4^2)$ grams in each pack. Find $c$ such that only 1% of packs weigh less than $c$. Then find the $\sigma$ needed so that only 1% weigh less than 245 g.

```{r}
qnorm(0.01, 250, 4)                # c = 240.69
z01 <- qnorm(0.99)                 # upper-tail point z_0.01 = 2.326
(250 - 245) / z01                  # sigma = 2.149
```

Draws and the density on top:

```{r}
set.seed(9)
draws <- rnorm(1000, mu, sigma)
hist(draws, breaks = 30, probability = TRUE, main = "1000 draws from N(170, 64)")
curve(dnorm(x, mu, sigma), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

## Exponential distribution

Orders arrive at rate $\lambda=0.5$ per minute; $T\sim\text{Exp}(0.5)$ is the time to the next order. `R` uses the **rate** $\lambda$ (mean $1/\lambda$).

```{r}
lambda <- 0.5
pexp(3, rate = lambda, lower.tail = FALSE)   # P(T > 3) = 0.223
qexp(0.5, rate = lambda)                     # median = log(2)/0.5 = 1.386
1 / lambda                                   # mean = 2 minutes
```

Memoryless property: $P(T>5\mid T>2)=P(T>3)$.

```{r}
pexp(5, lambda, lower.tail = FALSE) / pexp(2, lambda, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

Simulation check of the Poisson link: the number of orders in 3 minutes is $\text{Poisson}(1.5)$, and "no order in 3 minutes" is the same event as $T>3$.

```{r}
set.seed(9)
t1 <- rexp(1e5, lambda)
mean(t1 > 3)                 # simulated P(T > 3)
dpois(0, lambda * 3)         # P(N(3) = 0) = exp(-1.5)
```

## Gamma distribution

The time $T_3$ of the third order is $\text{Gamma}(\alpha=3,\lambda=0.5)$: the sum of three independent exponential gaps.

```{r}
pgamma(6, shape = 3, rate = 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE)  # P(T3 > 6) = 0.423
ppois(2, lambda = 0.5 * 6)                            # same: P(N(6) <= 2)
3 / 0.5                                               # mean = 6
3 / 0.5^2                                             # variance = 12
```

Shape controls skewness:

```{r}
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 1, rate = 0.5), 0, 25, ylab = "f(x)", lwd = 2,
      main = "Gamma densities, rate 0.5")
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 3, rate = 0.5), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 8, rate = 0.5), add = TRUE, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("shape 1 (exponential)", "shape 3", "shape 8"),
       col = c("black", "red", "blue"), lwd = 2)
```

Sum of exponentials, by simulation:

```{r}
set.seed(9)
t3 <- replicate(1e4, sum(rexp(3, rate = 0.5)))
hist(t3, breaks = 40, probability = TRUE, main = "Sum of 3 Exp(0.5) gaps")
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 3, rate = 0.5), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
mean(t3 > 6)                 # close to 0.423
```

**Exercise:** a help desk receives calls at rate 2 per hour. Let $T_4$ be the time of the 4th call. Compute $P(T_4\le 2)$ in two ways, with `pgamma` and with `ppois`.

```{r}
pgamma(2, shape = 4, rate = 2)   # 0.5665
1 - ppois(3, lambda = 2 * 2)     # same
```
